A tomato ripens through a predictable sequence of colours: green, then yellow, then orange, then red. The app samples thousands of pixels inside the focus box, converts each one to hue/saturation/brightness, throws away everything that cannot be tomato skin (grey backgrounds, deep shadows, glare, blue and violet surroundings), and sorts the rest into colour bands.\n\nEach band carries a ripeness weight, and their weighted average becomes a ripeness score from 0.00 (completely green) to 1.00 (completely red). That score picks the stage. Verdicts are voted across the last several frames so the reading does not flicker while you move the phone.

Unripe — score below 0.35. Still green; about a week to go.

Starting to turn — 0.35 to 0.60. Green giving way to yellow; roughly 3 to 5 days.

Almost ripe — 0.60 to 0.80. Mostly orange-red; one or two days.

Ripe — 0.80 and above. Fully red and ready to eat.

Overripe — deep red but dark and dull. Better cooked than eaten raw.

Colour analysis only.

No trained model is installed, so the stage comes purely from skin colour. This works well in even lighting on a single tomato that fills the focus box.

To add the trained model, run tools/train_ripeness_model.py on the Kaggle dataset and drop the resulting model.tflite and labels.txt into app/src/main/assets.

Trained model plus colour analysis.\n\nmodel.tflite decides whether the tomato is ripe or unripe — that is what the Kaggle dataset labels. Colour analysis then refines the answer into how many days are left, and confidence is reduced whenever the two methods disagree.

Colour is a good ripeness signal, but it is only the outside of the fruit:

• Coloured lighting shifts hues. Daylight or neutral white light gives the most reliable reading.

• Yellow, orange, green, and striped tomato varieties never turn red, so they read as unripe for their whole life.

• Ripeness is not the same as food safety. The app cannot see mould, bruising, splits, or spoilage inside the fruit. Always check and smell a tomato before eating it.

• Only the focus box is inspected, and only one tomato at a time.
Every frame is analysed on the device and discarded immediately. Nothing is recorded, stored, or sent anywhere, and the app needs no account and no internet connection.
Ripeness classes follow the “Riped and Unriped Tomato Dataset” by sumn2u on Kaggle, along with its companion YOLOv8 detection notebook.\n\nkaggle.com/datasets/sumn2u/riped-and-unriped-tomato-dataset
